SOP Version 1 - November 27, 2023, 4:45 PM
I want to study math. While my exposure to the field is limited, everything I have learned in my undergraduate career about logic has challenged me in a way I cannot get enough of. I saw Faculty Member’s research on blank and xxxxxx courses at xxxxxxxxx institution. I may not know much about these yet, but growing my knowledge in these fields sounds like the most fascinating direction for me.
I’ve currently completed the requirements for my undergraduate degree in mathematics at the Midwest University, and yet I find myself deeply unsatisfied with my current progress as a mathematician. I thought coming in that I would do my four years learning as much mathematics as I could and I would come out of it “knowing math”. I feel lucky to have an extra semester to take additional math courses at the undergraduate level purely for the sake of my interest, but it's clear to me that won’t give me what I’m looking for. I have so many questions about why mathematicians decided to create certain structures and how they interplay with one another. Beyond that, I have questions about how different fields are connected and just how generalized results can get. Honestly, I just want to feel like I know and understand something nontrivial about mathematics at a deep level. A doctorate degree feels like the best, maybe the only, way for me to achieve that.
                In my undergrad, I’ve already tried to take several courses that position me with a good background to learn more. Beyond the core classes necessary to graduate, I am currently taking an introductory logic course so that I can get an idea of what I hope to be doing. It’s primarily been an overview of model theory so far. I am in love with everything I’ve learned in this course, and while it is some of the hardest material for me so far, I want to do so much more with it. It’s obvious to me I want to continue to work with these kinds of questions. At your institution, this class seems like a good way to start that journey.
Learning the history of how a field developed is important to me as well, a skill I started to cultivate in my History of Mathematics course. I found that the more I understand about a field’s development, the easier it is for me to understand why certain structures or proofs are laid out how they are. In order to get an understanding of how logic developed as a field I did quite a bit of research into its history which culminated in a 15 minute talk I presented at City College’s Undergraduate Research Symposium. As much as I care about learning for the sake of learning, it all amounts to nothing if I can’t communicate those ideas clearly. 
As an older sister to a forever curious highschool student, I live for the 8pm calls asking me to explain why the real numbers aren’t countable, or why a derivative doesn’t work on a function that isn’t smooth, or what a function even is. While I’m extremely fortunate to have a little nerd in my life who wants to hear about everything I’m learning, tutoring calculus and statistics students has taught me how to communicate these things to audiences who are less than excited about the material. I would love to continue developing these skills through teaching opportunities at Name of your Institution.
Teaching may be one way I become familiar with math, but another is learning it collaboratively with people. At an undergraduate level, it’s difficult to find people who want to get excited about logic and want to learn it with me. While this may continue to prove difficult, being at an institution with other graduate students learning feels absolutely necessary for me to continue on my journey of mathematical growth. I need to figure out what I’m doing with this paragraph




··  Para 6: This is dedicated to all the social activities you have been involved in since you were born. US universities have a soft corner for social activities so make sure you do have something to write here! It can be anything from blood donation to some serious NGO work.


·  Para 7: Mention some of your co-curricular activities here, which show that you are not just a boring academic person, but also do have a life! This content makes the admission committee get to know you on a personal level, and it really helps them to form an image of you.

One thing, it may seem easy to lie in this paragraph, but please don't. The committee people have this uncanny ability to detect such lies, and trust me, if they think you are just boasting, it can have a negative impact.
·  Para 8: Ok, now according to my POV this is THE MOST IMPORTANT PARAGRAPH of your SOP. Here you have to tell the university people why the hell do you wanna go there!! As I said earlier, make sure you give them solid reasons for doing so. These reasons should get them thinking and admiring their university. You require a lot of research to write this para. I used to scan each and every word on the department website before even thinking to come out with my reasons.

Mention names of professors, labs, courses, facilities, projects and what not to get their attention.
·  Para 9: This is the conclusion of your SOP. Remember to be modest and be soft. Express your gratitude and humbly ask for scholarship if you want one. That should do it.
